items.question: Where should spiritual practice be rooted, in consciousness or in breath, body, and intellect?
premises: Practice is truly rooted within consciousness itself.
Through consciousness it may be extended to breath, body, or intellect.
The proper rule is to practice in consciousness, not merely in the lower supports.
items.inference: Because consciousness is the true ground, practice in breath, body, or intellect is secondary and valid only through consciousness.
uncertainties: The exact force of vārpyaṃ as 'to be placed' or 'to be sown' is slightly ambiguous.
items.plain_english: What is truly rooted is rooted within consciousness. Through that, practice may be applied to breath, body, or intellect, but by practicing in that way one does not follow the real rule. The real rule is to practice in consciousness itself.

rows.grounds: reason and effect of inclusive practice

items.question: Can practice in breath, intellect, or body still be valid from the nondual standpoint?
premises: In our view, breath, intellect, body, and the rest clearly share the nature of the all.
Because they are all-natured, practice situated in them is not excluded.
Such practice removes fixation on what is taken as other.
items.inference: From the nondual standpoint, practice in any of these supports can serve the removal of otherness because all are expressions of the same reality.
uncertainties: The sandhi-packed final compound allows slight variation in how tightly the causal and result clauses are joined.
items.plain_english: Or, in our view, breath, intellect, body, and the rest are clearly of the nature of the all. Because of that, even practice carried out in them removes the sense of otherness.

items.question: What enables the body to leap rather than remain held back by fear of falling?
premises: The body has an inner impulse toward rising that includes leaping and falling.
The body is made to leap when that impulse is active.
Leaping occurs through the removal of fear of falling to the opposite side.
items.inference: Action becomes possible when the mind's opposing fear is removed, allowing the body's rising impulse to express itself.
uncertainties: The long compound in the second token can be parsed with slightly different emphasis on 'nature' versus 'desire'.
items.plain_english: The body leaps because of an inner impulse to rise that naturally includes leaping and falling. It is made to leap when the fear of falling to the opposite side is removed.

items.question: What happens to opposing thoughts when self-reflection awakens in a way similar to the guru's word?
premises: Self-reflection can awaken in a form similar to reflection on the guru's word.
When that self-reflection is awakened, it does not coexist peacefully with its opposites.
In study and reflection, the opposites are rejected.
items.inference: Awakened self-reflection, resonant with the guru's word, naturally dispels contrary mental positions.
uncertainties: pāṭhacintane may refer specifically to textual study or more broadly to reflective recitation.
items.plain_english: When self-reflection awakens in a way similar to reflecting on the guru's word, the forces opposed to it are cast aside, even in the midst of study and reflection.

items.question: Can a guru implant one's own knowledge into the intellect by word alone?
premises: A guru cannot implant one's own knowledge into the intellect merely by word.
Knowledge that is truly one's own cannot be externally inserted as a finished product.
Therefore awakening must unfold through an inner sequence.
items.inference: Because knowledge cannot be implanted from outside by speech alone, genuine realization necessarily arises through self-awakening.
uncertainties: śabda eva vā could be read as emphasizing word alone or as contrasting word with another external means.
items.plain_english: A guru cannot place one's own knowledge into the intellect by word alone. For that reason, the unfolding of self-awakening is certain and necessary.

items.question: Does contemplating identity with something heard in a dream produce liberating fruit?
premises: A teaching or object may be heard even in a dream.
One may practice contemplative union by identifying with that dream content.
Such identification is not said to yield liberating fruit.
items.inference: Mere identification with received content, even when vivid, does not by itself produce the fruit of realization.
uncertainties: The verse may be targeting dream instruction specifically or any externally received content taken as sufficient.
items.plain_english: For this reason, even if something is heard in a dream and one practices union by contemplating identity with it, that is not said to bring real fruit.

items.question: What distinguishes mere recitation from contemplation of meaning?
premises: When convention is disregarded, reflection remains fixed on the word alone.
Reflection fixed on the word is called recitation.
When regard is given to meaning, the practice becomes contemplation of that meaning.
items.inference: Recitation and contemplation differ by whether attention rests on verbal form or on the meaning it conveys.
uncertainties: saṃketānādare may mean disregard for conventional meaning or simple non-attention to it.
items.plain_english: When there is no regard for convention, reflection stays fixed on the word, and that is recitation. When there is regard for it, attention turns to its meaning, and that is contemplation. This distinction should be carefully examined.

items.question: What is the real use of practice within nondual consciousness?
premises: Practice in that nondual consciousness is not useless.
Its purpose is limited rather than productive of nonduality itself.
It serves to uproot doubt caused by the stain of duality.
items.inference: Practice does not create nondual consciousness but removes the lingering doubt of duality that obscures it.
uncertainties: mālinya may suggest a moral stain or more generally a contaminating obscuration.
items.plain_english: Practice in that nondual consciousness is not useless. Its sole purpose is to uproot the doubt that arises from the stain of duality.

items.question: How are doubts of duality removed, and what role do disciplines like yama play in that process?
premises: Doubts of duality are examined and resolved through reasoning.
This has already been stated in the teaching.
Disciplines such as yama can serve as means for establishing that reasoning.
items.inference: Reasoning directly addresses doubts of duality, while disciplines like yama are useful only insofar as they support that reasoning.
uncertainties: tarkyanta can suggest being reasoned about, tested, or dispelled through reasoning.
items.plain_english: It has been said that doubts about duality are resolved through reasoning. Disciplines such as yama are useful too, but only as supports for establishing that reasoning.

items.question: What does the earlier scripture say about duality, nonduality, and ritual worship?
premises: The revered earlier scripture addresses the ultimate status of practice and doctrine.
It negates both duality and nonduality as final positions.
It includes linga worship and similar practices within that sweeping statement by Shambhu.
items.inference: The cited scripture relativizes both doctrinal opposites and ritual forms rather than granting any of them final authority.
uncertainties: The verse is introductory, so the full force of the negation depends on the following verse.
items.plain_english: In the revered earlier scripture, Shambhu begins by saying that neither duality nor nonduality, nor even linga worship and the like, has final standing.

items.question: Why are prescribed and prohibited practices, including yogic limbs, said to be artificial here?
premises: In this scriptural context, everything prescribed is also, in another respect, prohibited.
Yogas consisting of limbs such as breath control fall within that same field.
Because they are constructed and rule-bound, they are artificial.
items.inference: Rule-based yogic practices are limited and artificial because they depend on injunction and prohibition rather than on the unconstructed reality.
uncertainties: The verse compresses a strong polemic; the exact scope of 'all' may be rhetorical within the cited scripture.
items.plain_english: Here, everything that is prescribed is also, in another way, prohibited. Yogas made up of limbs such as breath control would therefore be artificial, because they are constructed.

items.question: If artificial practices fall short of the uncreated reality, why are they still prescribed at all?
premises: Artificial practices are not worth even a sixteenth part of the uncreated reality.
Their value is therefore radically limited in comparison with the uncreated.
Even so, they may still be prescribed here by rule for a certain purpose.
items.inference: Constructed practices have no ultimate parity with the uncreated, yet they can still be conventionally prescribed within a regulated framework.
uncertainties: The verse states that prescription remains but does not specify its exact pedagogical purpose.
items.plain_english: Therefore these artificial practices are not worth even a sixteenth part of that uncreated reality. Still, O Goddess, they are prescribed here by rule.
